newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIAN OPPOSITION WILL CONSIDER TAX PLANS.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIAN OPPOSITION WILL CONSIDER TAX PLANS.

text.p: The Australian opposition on Wednesday said it would consider any government proposals for tax reform but also criticised the option of a broad-based indirect tax.

However, Opposition Leader Kim Beazley, responding to Prime Minister John Howard's announcement of an inquiry into tax reform, refused to declare unqualified opposition to such a goods and services tax.
"We're happy to look at tax," Beazley told reporters.
"What we want to see is a focus on this government on jobs. We want to see what their proposals are."
A goods and services tax (GST) would hurt families, small business and the jobs it generated, Beazley said.
When directly asked "Are you implacably against a GST?" he merely repeated his criticisms of the option.
But he later said that while the Labor opposition would not raise the GST as an issue for the election due before mid 1999 it would certainly fight it if it became an issue.
Earlier on Wednesday, Howard ensured that the election would be fought at least partly over tax by ordering the bureaucratic inquiry and promising to reveal a policy before the country votes.
Howard has long favoured a GST and reaffirmed on Wednesday that he had "a very clear view" of the right direction for reform.
The ruling Liberal-National coalition last proposed a GST -- a 15 percent value-added tax -- in 1991 and consequently lost the 1993 election.

Critics describe the current Australian tax system as an incoherent mess. Federal income tax carries a high burden -- with marginal rates rising rapidly to almost 50 percent, encouraging avoidance -- while indirect taxes apply unevenly on some goods but almost no services.
The state governments survive on federal grants and a variety of small taxes with very little breadth -- for example, on payrolls, real estate sales and vehicle fuel.
The Australian Democrats -- a minor party that can deliver crucial votes in parliament -- said the government was merely trying to look like it was taking action to help it win the election.
The Democrats also opposed the previous GST proposal as inequitable and their leader, Cheryl Kernot, said on Wednesday any new plan would be equally unfair to some people.
Beazely predicted the government would try to attract voters to a high-rate GST by offering small cuts to income tax.
"What is being proposed here is a few cents shaved off, or a change in the basis of your brackets, in return for which you get to pay ... a goods and services tax of 20 percent plus," he said.
Howard did not say when the inquiry would report.
Recent opinion polls have shown the government's once commanding lead over the opposition slipping away.
The Reuters Poll Trend, a smoothed average of the polls, shows that if an election were held now the government would survive with a greatly reduced majority.
-- Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
